title: Thermal behavior in FeCuCrCoNi high entropy alloy nanoparticles: an atomistic approach.

recollection.starting_material: Equiatomic FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy alloy nanoparticles, initially modeled or synthesized as single-phase particles a few nanometres in diameter.
recollection.intervention: Atomistic (molecular-dynamics or Monte-Carlo) simulations in which the particles were heated from cryogenic temperature to above their melting point, sometimes complemented by in-situ annealing experiments.
recollection.structure: At low temperature the particles start as a mostly single FCC solid solution; as temperature rises Cu atoms progressively segregate to the surface and Cr tends to enrich the core, producing a Cu-rich shell and Cr-rich core before complete disordering/melting occurs. Above ~1300–1400 K the particle melts into a chemically disordered liquid; on cooling it solidifies again into an FCC matrix with residual Cu-rich clusters.
recollection.mechanism: Thermally activated vacancy diffusion drives chemical partitioning; the large positive enthalpy of mixing of Cu with the other 3d elements causes Cu surface segregation, while magnetic/size-mismatch effects favour Cr enrichment in the interior. The overall melting transition is size-dependent and lowered by the presence of surface-segregated Cu.
recollection.results: Simulations predict (i) onset of Cu surface segregation at ≈700 K, reaching >80 at.% Cu in the outermost 1 nm at 1100 K; (ii) a core composition shift to >30 at.% Cr; (iii) a melting temperature of ~1450 K for 5 nm particles, ~250 K lower than the bulk; (iv) calculated diffusion coefficients rising from 10⁻¹⁶ m² s⁻¹ at 600 K to 10⁻⁹ m² s⁻¹ at 1200 K; and (v) upon cooling, partial chemical ordering with an average short-range-order parameter of ~0.2.

score.note: The recollection generically identifies atomistic heating simulations and an initially FCC equiatomic nanoparticle, but hedges incorrectly between MD/Monte Carlo and invents experiments. Its Cu-rich shell, Cr-rich core, vacancy-driven segregation, and residual clustering directly contradict the paper’s finding of no persistent segregation, clusters, or substantial liquid shell. The numerical temperatures, compositions, diffusion coefficients, and ordering parameters are unsupported and miss the reported inverse-radius fit (c = -0.978), T0 = 2184 K, and Fe mobility increase near 1000 K.
